lead: A circuit with several sources can be solved one source at a time. In a linear circuit, every voltage and current is a weighted sum of the independent source values, so the response to all sources together equals the sum of the responses to each source acting alone. That is the superposition theorem. It explains why a small signal can ride on a DC bias, why an audio mixer adds its inputs, and why one source can be studied while the others are switched off. It applies to voltages and currents, never directly to power.
prereq: You need: mesh analysis or nodal analysis, and series-parallel reduction.

blocks.text: Treat each independent source as an input x and any chosen voltage or current as the output y. A circuit is linear when it has two properties.

items: Homogeneity (scaling): multiply every input by k and the output is multiplied by k.
Additivity: the output for inputs x₁ and x₂ together is the output for x₁ alone plus the output for x₂ alone.

blocks.text: Resistors (v = Ri), inductors (v = L di/dt) and capacitors (i = C dv/dt) are linear elements: each relation is linear in the element's own variables. A dependent source with a constant gain (μ, g, r or β) is linear too. Diodes, transistors driven into saturation and lamps whose resistance changes with temperature are not.

y is any voltage or current in the circuit; x<sub>k</sub> is the value of independent source k; a<sub>k</sub> is a constant set by the resistances and dependent-source gains; N is the number of independent sources.

Why it holds: nodal or mesh analysis of a linear circuit gives equations whose coefficients are fixed numbers and whose right sides contain only the source values. The solution of such equations is a weighted sum of the right sides. Homogeneity also gives a short method for ladder networks, the unit-output method: assume 1 A (or 1 V) in the far branch, work back to the source value this needs, then scale everything by the true source value.

items: List the independent sources. Keep one and switch off all the others.

Switch off a voltage source by making it 0 V: replace it by a short circuit (a wire). Switch off a current source by making it 0 A: replace it by an open circuit (a gap). Any internal resistance stays in place.
Leave every dependent source in the circuit, still controlled by its variable.
Solve the reduced circuit for the wanted voltage or current, marking its sign against a fixed reference direction.
Repeat for each independent source in turn, then add the partial answers with their signs.

blocks.text: y = y′ + y″ + … (one term per source)
blocks.where: y′ is the response with only the first independent source on, y″ with only the second, and so on.

blocks.text: Sources may also be switched on in groups, as long as every source is on in exactly one run. Superposition usually takes more work than one nodal solution for a plain DC circuit; its real uses are to show how much each source contributes, to handle sources of different frequencies (see applying network theorems to AC circuits), and to prove the other theorems of this unit.

Power does not superpose. Power is P = I²R or V²/R, a square, and (I′ + I″)²R = I′²R + 2I′I″R + I″²R. The cross term 2I′I″R is missing if you add the partial powers. In worked example 1 the partial powers add to 27 W, but the true power is 54 W. Superpose the current or voltage first, then compute power once.

Dependent sources must not be switched off. Their value is set by a voltage or current that changes from run to run, so they stay in every reduced circuit. In worked example 2, switching off the controlled source gives 9.33 V instead of the correct 9 V.
Nonlinear elements break it. A diode's current is not a weighted sum of the source values, so superposition holds only for small changes about a fixed operating point (the small-signal model).

examples.question: A 12 V source in series with a 2 Ω resistor feeds node A. A 6 Ω resistor joins A to the reference, and a 6 A current source drives current from the reference into A (Figure 2.3.1). Find V<sub>A</sub> by superposition, then the power in the 6 Ω resistor. Compare with the sum of the two partial powers.
steps: Run 1, 12 V alone: open the 6 A source. The 2 Ω and 6 Ω are in series: I = 12/(2 + 6) = 1.5 A, so V<sub>A</sub>′ = 1.5 × 6 = 9 V.
Run 2, 6 A alone: short the 12 V source. The 2 Ω now runs from A to the reference, in parallel with the 6 Ω: 2 × 6/(2 + 6) = 1.5 Ω. V<sub>A</sub>″ = 6 × 1.5 = 9 V.
Add: V<sub>A</sub> = 9 + 9 = 18 V (both runs make A positive).
Check by nodal analysis with both sources on: (V<sub>A</sub> − 12)/2 + V<sub>A</sub>/6 = 6. Times 6: 3V<sub>A</sub> − 36 + V<sub>A</sub> = 36, so V<sub>A</sub> = 18 V.
Partial powers: 9²/6 = 13.5 W in each run, sum 27 W. The difference, 27 W, is the cross term 2 × (9 × 9)/6 = 27 W.
examples.answer: V<sub>A</sub> = 18 V and the 6 Ω resistor takes 54 W; adding the partial powers would wrongly give 27 W.

examples.question: A 10 V source in series with 2 Ω feeds node a; iₓ is the current in the 2 Ω towards a. From a to the reference there are a 4 Ω resistor and a current-controlled current source of 0.5iₓ that draws current out of a. A 2 A source drives current from the reference into a. Find the voltage v of node a by superposition.
steps: KCL at a in every run: current in through the 2 Ω + source current in = current out through the 4 Ω + 0.5iₓ, with iₓ = (V<sub>s</sub> − v)/2 where V<sub>s</sub> is the value of the 10 V source in that run.
Run 1, 10 V alone (2 A source open): iₓ = (10 − v)/2 and iₓ = v/4 + 0.5iₓ, so 0.5iₓ = v/4, giving (10 − v)/4 = v/4 and v′ = 5 V (iₓ′ = 2.5 A).
Run 2, 2 A alone (10 V source shorted): iₓ = (0 − v)/2 = −v/2 and iₓ + 2 = v/4 + 0.5iₓ, so 0.5iₓ + 2 = v/4, giving −v/4 + 2 = v/4 and v″ = 4 V (iₓ″ = −2 A). The controlled source stays in this run.
Check with both sources: iₓ = (10 − 9)/2 = 0.5 A; in = 0.5 + 2 = 2.5 A; out = 9/4 + 0.5 × 0.5 = 2.25 + 0.25 = 2.5 A. KCL holds.
Wrong method for comparison: switching off the controlled source in each run gives 10 × 4/6 = 6.67 V and 2 × (2 ∥ 4) = 2.67 V, total 9.33 V, which fails the KCL check.
examples.answer: v = 9 V (5 V from the 10 V source and 4 V from the 2 A source), with iₓ = 0.5 A.

traps: Shorting a current source or opening a voltage source to switch it off. Off means 0 V (short) for a voltage source and 0 A (open) for a current source.
Switching off a dependent source. It stays in every run; worked example 2 shows the error (9.33 V instead of 9 V).
Adding powers. Add currents or voltages, then square once: 54 W, not 27 W, in worked example 1.
Dropping a sign. Draw one reference direction for the wanted current before the first run and give every partial answer a sign against it.
Removing a source's internal resistance along with the source. Only the ideal source is replaced; a 0.5 Ω internal resistance stays.

quiz.q: Name the two properties that together make a circuit linear.
How do you switch off an ideal voltage source and an ideal current source for superposition?
quiz.a: Voltage source: replace by a short circuit (0 V). Current source: replace by an open circuit (0 A).

quiz.q: Why must a dependent source stay on in every run?
quiz.a: Its value is set by a voltage or current in the circuit, which differs from run to run. Removing it removes a real part of every response, so the partial answers no longer add up to the true one.

quiz.q: In worked example 1, the 12 V source is raised to 24 V. Use homogeneity to find the new V<sub>A</sub>.
quiz.a: Run 1 doubles to 2 × 9 = 18 V; run 2 is still 9 V. V<sub>A</sub> = 27 V. Check: (27 − 24)/2 + 27/6 = 1.5 + 4.5 = 6 A.

quiz.q: Two sources drive a 4 Ω resistor. Source 1 alone gives 3 A downward; source 2 alone gives 5 A upward. Find the current and the power.
quiz.a: Downward positive: 3 − 5 = −2 A, so 2 A upward. P = 2² × 4 = 16 W. Adding partial powers (36 + 100 = 136 W) is wrong.

quiz.q: A student adds 13.5 W and 13.5 W and reports 27 W in the 6 Ω resistor of worked example 1. Explain the error in terms of the cross term.
quiz.a: P = (V′ + V″)²/R = V′²/R + 2V′V″/R + V″²/R. The cross term 2 × 9 × 9/6 = 27 W is missing, so the true power is 27 + 27 = 54 W.

beyond: Superposition is the basis of small-signal analysis: an amplifier is solved once for its DC bias and once for the small AC signal, and the two are added. Power engineers add each generator's contribution to a fault current, and signal-integrity engineers add the crosstalk from each neighbouring line. Search for 'small-signal model', 'fault current contribution' and 'crosstalk superposition'.
